sentences.text: This episode features the second portion of our conversation with the award winning literary translator, Jennifer Fe Lee.
Where last time we learned about her journey to Cantonese and her work translating the poetry and prose of the Hong Kong author, She She.
This time we hear about her recent translation of the psychological thriller Tongeless by Lao Yue.
Set in a Hong Kong secondary school, it zeroes in on the pressure cooker environment faced by contract teachers as they navigate the shifting linguistic landscape between Cantonese and Mandarin.
Make sure to tune in next time for the third and final installment of our conversation, where Jennifer shares tips for getting into literary translation.
But what I really appreciated is that my editor, even from the first drops, she got it.
So there's a point in the novel when these teachers who have been teaching Chinese and Cantonese are being pressured to take these exams and to prove their proficiency in Mandarin.
So they're having a lunch with this principal from Nanjing and they're asked to introduce themselves in Mandarin.
So these characters who you might have known as Miss Ng or Miss Wu or Miss Yip, suddenly now you're learning that Miss Wu is Miss Hu, Miss Ng is Miss Wu, Miss Yip is Miss Ye and so on.
My editor made a comment in the margin, she said, this is very sinister.
And I loved that she got it because this was not a person who was coming to this from a background in Chinese studies or Hong Kong studies.
But she could still tell that this has some very, there was something sinister about the undertone to her.
And I love that she got that. And I hope other readers will get this.
I hope they do too, also because the other thing that I think is so fascinating about the novel is, yes, it does deal with the language politics in a really interesting way.
But it also touches on a ton of other social issues in Hong Kong with an incredible depth and complexity that I think for people who've lived in Hong Kong will resonate very deeply.

But also for people who maybe don't know as much about Hong Kong, it's a great opportunity to learn some things, whether it's about the property market, immigration complications and sort of what it's like for people who immigrated to Hong Kong from the mainland,
whether 40 years ago or in the past couple years.

Like what's the, what's the quick pitch you've given to maybe English readers to try and get them to think about picking up the book?

And I think it makes a really interesting contrast to some other recent depictions of Hong Kong in the media.
Yeah.I mean, what, I don't know if we should name them or not, but we all can probably think of some.
I think a lot of people probably know Hong Kong through visual media.

But sometimes literature, Hong Kong literature in particular, sort of helps make sort of the invisible visible.
Yes.And I wonder if there's anything in particular that you find being made very visible in Tonglass.
Yes.I mean, the author herself, I mean, I can kind of cheat because, you know, I saw the materials that she was preparing for agents and for publishers in Taiwan explaining the book.

And one of the things that she really stressed when she was trying to pitch the book to the Taiwan market or to literary agents was the fact that this is one of the rare books to talk about politically apathetic people in Hong Kong.
Because I think right now there's a lot of interest in people who have been part of the protest, you know, into people who are writing about these very important movements in Hong Kong.
But her characters, I think there's one point where one of the protagonist thing is even annoyed by the protest because it makes it harder to get to work.
You know, she's more obsessed with beauty treatments in these luxury fashion brands.
And this other character of why is just obsessed with learning Mandarin.
Of course, you can bring in a lot of political readings to the book, but the characters themselves are not these activists.
They're not really engaging, at least overtly with the politics around them.

And so I think that's very interesting because in fact, I think there are a lot of people in Hong Kong who perhaps at least outwardly were sort of, they were not necessarily engaging with the protest.
They were just living their lives, you know, trying to get by.
Maybe they for certain reasons, they didn't want to express their opinions one way or the other.
But I have found in my own experience when I'm trying to get works from Hong Kong published in English.
I don't want, I don't want to generalize, but I have noticed that publishers often times are gravitating either towards works that are surrealistic or overtly political.
And so the works that might be have a more realist spent but are not necessarily directly engaging with politics.
I'm seeing those often have a harder time to find a home.
And I think it's really interesting because this book, I mean the characters, they really, whether it's because they,
are so desperate just to survive that they can't imagine, you know, engaging with what's going on beyond this.
